title: Should every microservice publish an event for every database change — no, events are CONTRACTS that create dependencies just like APIs — publishing every table mutation as a public event stream exposes persistence internals, makes schema evolution painful, and couples consumers to the producer's internal model — instead, publish events representing meaningful DOMAIN FACTS that other components legitimately need, and treat the event schema as a versioned integration contract (not a DB changelog)?
shortTitle: Should every microservice publish an event for every database change

s1_definition.profdef: No — a service should not publish an event for every database change, because a published event is a contract exactly like a public API: every consumer couples to it, so broadcasting every table mutation as a public stream exposes your persistence internals, makes schema evolution painful, and ties consumers to your internal data model. Instead you publish events that represent meaningful domain facts other components legitimately need, deliberately designed and versioned as integration contracts, rather than emitting a raw database changelog where every column change becomes a public event.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine every time National Bank of India's transfer department scribbled anything in its internal notebook — a draft figure, a corrected typo, an intermediate status — it photocopied that page and mailed it to every other department. The other departments would start depending on those scribbles, so the transfer team could never tidy its notebook without breaking everyone. The right approach is that the transfer department only sends an official announcement when something truly meaningful happens, like "a transfer completed," on a clean standardized form. The notebook stays private and editable; only deliberate domain facts become announcements everyone can rely on.
s1_definition.oneliner: Events are contracts like APIs, so publish deliberate, versioned domain facts that consumers need — not a raw changelog of every table mutation.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** No — a service should not publish an event for every database change, because a published event is a contract exactly like a public API: every consumer couples to it, so broadcasting every table mutation as a public stream exposes your persistence internals, makes schema evolution painful, and ties consumers to your internal data model. Instead you publish events that represent meaningful domain facts other components legitimately need, deliberately designed and versioned as integration contracts, rather than emitting a raw database changelog where every column change becomes a public event.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine every time National Bank of India's transfer department scribbled anything in its internal notebook — a draft figure, a corrected typo, an intermediate status — it photocopied that page and mailed it to every other department. The other departments would start depending on those scribbles, so the transfer team could never tidy its notebook without breaking everyone. The right approach is that the transfer department only sends an official announcement when something truly meaningful happens, like "a transfer completed," on a clean standardized form. The notebook stays private and editable; only deliberate domain facts become announcements everyone can rely on.

**One line to remember:** Events are contracts like APIs, so publish deliberate, versioned domain facts that consumers need — not a raw changelog of every table mutation.

sections.s2_technical:
The tempting idea is to wire change data capture straight onto every table and publish every insert, update, and delete as a public event, so other services can react to anything. It feels decoupled because the producer does not call anyone, but it is a trap, because a published event is a contract. The instant a consumer subscribes and reads fields from your event, those fields and their meaning are part of an agreement you must honor, exactly like a REST API's response shape. If your events are simply your table rows, then your database schema has become your public API, and you have coupled every consumer to your persistence internals.

The concrete harms follow directly. Exposure of internals: internal columns, staging states, denormalizations, and implementation details you never intended to be external are now visible and depended upon. Painful schema evolution: you can no longer rename a column, split a table, change a type, or refactor your storage without risking breakage in services owned by other teams, so the freedom to evolve your own data model — one of the main benefits of database-per-service — is gone. Semantic noise: consumers receive a flood of low-level mutations, many of which are intermediate or meaningless, and must reverse-engineer business meaning from raw row changes, which is fragile. Tight coupling: the whole point of events was loose coupling, and raw-changelog events deliver the opposite.

The correct approach is to publish events that represent meaningful domain facts — things that happened in the business that other components legitimately care about, like TransferCompleted, AccountFrozen, or LoanApproved. These are deliberately designed, named in business terms, carry only the curated fields consumers need, and are versioned as integration contracts using a schema format like Avro or Protobuf with a Schema Registry. A single business operation that touches five rows in three tables produces one domain-fact event, not fifteen row-change events. This keeps the event stream meaningful, keeps your internal schema private and free to evolve behind the stable event contract, and gives consumers exactly the facts they need.

There is an important distinction from change data capture itself. CDC and the transactional outbox are excellent mechanisms, but you point them at an outbox table that you fill with deliberately designed domain-fact events, not at your business tables directly. So CDC publishes the curated events you chose to emit; it does not turn every table mutation into a public event. This is the difference between using the database log as reliable transport for your chosen events versus leaking your schema as the contract.

A senior engineer frames it as treating the event catalog with the same discipline as the public API catalog. You decide deliberately what domain facts to publish, you own their schemas as contracts, you version them, and you keep them small and business-meaningful. Everything else — intermediate states, internal bookkeeping, storage shape — stays private. The guiding question for any proposed event is: does another component legitimately need to know this business fact, and am I willing to support this as a versioned contract forever? If not, it should not be a public event.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India's transfer service persists a transfer through several intermediate row updates and must decide what to publish.

Problem 1 — The naive approach publishes every row change: transfer row inserted as DRAFT, updated to VALIDATING, updated to RISK_CHECKED, an internal ledger row inserted, the transfer updated to COMPLETED. Five public events for one transfer, exposing internal states like DRAFT and VALIDATING and an internal ledger row. Consumers would start depending on these internals, and the transfer team could never change its state machine. This is the raw-changelog anti-pattern.

Problem 2 — The correct approach publishes exactly one meaningful domain fact when the business operation finishes: TransferCompleted, carrying only the curated fields consumers need. The intermediate states remain private implementation details.

Problem 3 — The event is a versioned contract, so even as the transfer team adds internal states or refactors tables, the TransferCompleted schema stays stable and consumers are unaffected.

What the code will do: a runnable demo runs one transfer through its internal state machine, producing several internal row changes. `RawChangelogPublisher` demonstrates the anti-pattern by emitting a public event for every mutation and logging warnings about leaked internals. `DomainFactPublisher` demonstrates the correct approach by emitting a single versioned TransferCompleted event with only curated fields. A `ConsumerView` shows how many events each approach forces on consumers and what internals leak.

```bash
# Real service

            "table.include.list":"public.outbox"}}'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one transfer T-123 for Rs.50000 that moves through internal states DRAFT, VALIDATING, RISK_CHECKED, an internal ledger insert, then COMPLETED.

Step 1 (raw changelog): As the state machine runs, the raw publisher emits a public event for every single mutation — the DRAFT status, the VALIDATING status, the RISK_CHECKED status, the internal ledger row, and the COMPLETED status. Five public events for one business operation.

Step 2 (raw changelog): The consumer receives all five. Four of them are internal states and an internal ledger table that it now sees and could start depending on. The report shows multiple row events and leaked internals, which means the transfer team can no longer change its state machine or tables without risk.

Step 3 (domain fact): The state machine runs the same internal mutations, but the domain-fact publisher keeps every internal mutation private, logging them only at fine level, and does not publish them.

Step 4 (domain fact): When the business operation actually completes, the publisher emits exactly one versioned TransferCompleted event carrying only the curated fields — transfer ID, account, beneficiary, amount.

Step 5 (domain fact): The consumer receives exactly one meaningful business event and sees no internals. The report shows one fact event and no leaked internals, so the transfer team is free to refactor its internals behind the stable contract.

Final output:

```
15:30:00 INFO    ===== RAW CHANGELOG (anti-pattern): publish every row change =====
15:30:00 WARNING [RAW] public event: transfer.status=DRAFT (leaks internals)
15:30:00 WARNING [RAW] public event: transfer.status=VALIDATING (leaks internals)
15:30:00 WARNING [RAW] public event: transfer.status=RISK_CHECKED (leaks internals)
15:30:00 WARNING [RAW] public event: internal_ledger.entry=T-123-leg1 (leaks internals)
15:30:00 WARNING [RAW] public event: transfer.status=COMPLETED (leaks internals)
15:30:00 INFO    [CONSUMER RAW_CHANGELOG] rowEvents=6 factEvents=0 leakedInternals=[transfer.DRAFT, transfer.VALIDATING, transfer.RISK_CHECKED, internal_ledger.T-123-leg1]
15:30:00 INFO    ===== DOMAIN FACT (correct): one meaningful business event =====
15:30:00 INFO    [FACT] public event: TransferCompleted v1 { T-124, SAV2001, BENEF-77, Rs.50000 }
15:30:00 INFO    [CONSUMER DOMAIN_FACT] rowEvents=0 factEvents=1 leakedInternals=[]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
No, a service should not publish an event for every database change, and the reason is that a published event is a contract, exactly like a public API. The moment a consumer subscribes and reads fields from your event, those fields and their meaning become an agreement you must honor. So if your events are just your table rows streamed out, then your database schema has silently become your public API, and you have coupled every consumer to your persistence internals — which is the precise opposite of what events are supposed to buy you.

The harms of the raw-changelog approach are concrete. It exposes internals — staging states, denormalizations, internal tables — that you never intended to be external but that consumers now depend on. It makes schema evolution painful, because you can no longer rename a column, split a table, or change a type without risking breakage in services owned by other teams, which throws away the main benefit of database-per-service, namely the freedom to evolve your own data model. It creates semantic noise, because consumers get a flood of low-level mutations, many of them intermediate and meaningless, and have to reverse-engineer business meaning from raw row changes. And it produces exactly the tight coupling events were meant to eliminate.

The right approach is to publish events that represent meaningful domain facts — things that actually happened in the business that other components legitimately need, like TransferCompleted, AccountFrozen, or LoanApproved. I design these deliberately, name them in business terms, include only the curated fields consumers need, and version them as integration contracts with Avro or Protobuf and a Schema Registry. One business operation that touches several rows in several tables produces one domain-fact event, not a dozen row-change events. I still use change data capture and the transactional outbox, but I point them at an outbox table I fill with deliberately chosen domain facts, never at my business tables directly, so CDC transports the events I chose rather than leaking my schema.

I enforced this at National Bank of India. Our transfer moves through internal states like DRAFT, VALIDATING, and RISK_CHECKED and writes an internal ledger row before reaching COMPLETED. Publishing every one of those mutations would have exposed our internal state machine and ledger table, and consumers would have started depending on states we needed to be free to change. Instead we keep all of that private and publish a single versioned TransferCompleted event with only the account, beneficiary, and amount, so the notification and statement teams get one clean, meaningful fact, and we can refactor our internal states and tables whenever we like behind that stable contract.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is this: events are contracts just like APIs, so I never publish every table mutation as a public stream, because that leaks internals and freezes my schema; instead I publish deliberate, versioned, business-meaningful domain facts that consumers genuinely need, CDC an outbox of those facts rather than my business tables, and keep every internal mutation private.
